notes: Evals 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 are self-contained: their fixtures live in evals/fixtures/ inside this skill (4 reuses 1; 5 targets partial failure and loops; 6 is the clean false-positive control; 7 distinguishes actual defenses from independent refund and failed-payment recovery defects; 9 tests an unverified re-audit antecedent; 10 tests independent root causes, historical snapshots and impact-based severity). Isolate runs to prevent stale reports; for re-audits seed the correct previous report. No expected finding count forbids additional evidence-backed defects. Assertions evaluate causal evidence and impact, not agreement with a preferred phrasing. Output selection is tested separately: cases 1-10 explicitly request full to preserve their detailed-format assertions; 11 uses no mode and must default to functional; 12 explicitly requests full on the same invoice fixture; 13 reauds an older full report in default functional mode. Every workspace now also holds tests.json; a scope with no tests records the suite as absent, so every invariant is uncovered and every finding undetected. Evals 17-20 close the remaining coverage gaps: 17 (stock-reservations) has an implicit machine, positive concurrency and system-limit findings, a justified critical and a suite with traps plus a red test that detects a defect; 18 (monorepo) must stop at needs_scope and use graphify to propose the stateful subsystem; 19 runs focused on billing/ with graphify in full mode and an absent suite; 20 needs setup — copy evals/fixtures/collision/orders-module.md to <working-dir>/systemic-out/orders-module.md BEFORE the run — and covers a name collision, the explicit standard profile and explicitly excluded tests. evals/COVERAGE.md maps every behavior the skill verifies to the evals and deterministic tests that cover it. Eval 22 must run where python3 is not on PATH; grade its workspace afterwards with Python. Evals 24 and 25 are the HELD-OUT set (split: holdout; every other case is dev). Run them to measure a change, never to tune the skill's wording: if one fails, fix the general instruction or add a dev fixture that shows the same weakness, and leave the holdout case as it is. 24 is the only fixture not written in Python (JavaScript, node:test) and exercises the validator's technique markers in another language; 25 has its defenses in a SQL schema and a single compare-and-set transition function, with one planted drift. evals.expected_output: A report following the skill's exact structure that models the orders system (elements, operators, declared vs built machine) and covers the seeded obligations without imposing a maximum finding count with file:line evidence, honesty labels and calibrated severities, plus a missing-piece synthesis.
assertions: Detects the closure violation: refund() writes status 'refund_pending' which is not in the STATUS set (models.py vs operations.py) — rated critical or high

Detects that mark_paid() sets paid_at/status without any guard on the current status (a draft order can become paid), either as its own finding or named as a manifestation of the one missing-guards finding — rated critical or high; the missing amount check is separate if reported
Detects the declared-vs-built contradiction: cancel() has no guard while the README forbids canceling a shipped order — rated critical or high
Detects the ambiguous operator: apply_discount() switches semantics on value<=1 (fraction vs absolute) while the README says percentage 0-100 — rated critical or high (value=1.0 zeroes the total)
Detects the broken symmetry: hold() exists but no release/resume operation exists anywhere in the module — rated high (paused orders have no exit, blocking business flow)

Detects the unreachable state: in_review is declared (README + STATUS) but no operation ever produces it — rated medium as a dead component, or high when the report shows that every payment skips the declared anti-fraud review (a demonstrated violation of a business rule); not critical

Detects the idempotency flaw: handle_payment_webhook() has no dedup by event_id although the README warns the provider retries/duplicates — rated critical or high (duplicate Payment records and an inflated total_paid)
Detects the double source of truth: Order.total stored while calc_total() exists, and add_item() does not update total — rated high (the webhook decides paid using the drifting stored total)
Detects the partial-failure risk in ship(): inventory reserved, courier.notify may raise, status not yet written, no transaction/compensation — rated critical or high

Severities are calibrated by demonstrated impact, not uniform or domain labels: unreachable in_review is medium or high with its justification, never critical; a critical rating needs supported severe consequences. No critical finding is mandatory solely because money or persisted data is involved.

The missing guards of mark_paid, cancel, ship, hold and checkout against the one declared lifecycle are ONE finding (the declared machine is enforced nowhere), naming each operator and its worst consequence as a manifestation and rated by the worst one; refund's undeclared status stays a separate closure finding, and the missing amount check stays separate if reported.

evals.name: saga-compensations-and-loops
evals.prompt: Run a systemic analysis of the booking saga at <SKILL_DIR>/evals/fixtures/booking-saga/ (README.md, steps.py, saga.py, worker.py). It runs across three external providers with no shared transaction and I am worried about what happens when a step fails. Use output full.
evals.expected_output: A report that models the saga as a system, maps each step to its compensation, and concentrates on partial failure (check 6) and feedback loops (check 12) — the two checks the other fixtures barely exercise — with file:line evidence, honesty labels and severities.
assertions: Detects the compensation off-by-one: _compensate_from() slices STEPS[:i-1] instead of STEPS[:i], so the step immediately before the failure is never compensated (saga.py, _compensate_from)
Traces the off-by-one to money: when reserve_hotel fails, charge_card is never compensated, so the customer stays charged for a trip that was not booked — contradicting the guarantee and rule 3
Detects that a failure in the FIRST step makes STEPS[:i-1] evaluate to STEPS[:-1], compensating two steps that never ran (releasing a null flight_ref and refunding a null charge_ref)
Detects that the compensation loop has no error handling: a compensation that raises skips every remaining compensation and leaves no record (saga.py, _compensate_from)
Detects that no saga state is ever persisted: booking.completed lives in memory and is never written, so a crash between steps leaves the invariant with no maintainer
Detects that booking.completed is appended to but never read by the compensation logic — a tracked source of truth the recovery path ignores
Detects the retry amplification in handle(): an unbounded while True with no backoff that ALSO re-enqueues the same booking on every failure, so each failure multiplies the work (worker.py, handle)
Detects the alert feedback loop: every failure notifies on-call, and on_alert() re-enqueues the booking, so the alert causes the action that causes the alert (worker.py, handle + on_alert)
Detects the dead-letter loop: drain_dead_letter() re-enqueues everything with no filter and nothing verifies the underlying problem was fixed, contrary to rule 6 (worker.py, drain_dead_letter)
Detects that nothing ever writes to the dead-letter queue although rule 6 declares it: drain_dead_letter() drains a queue no operator fills

Describes timeout-driven retry as conditional on cumulative provider latency exceeding TIMEOUT_SECONDS=2. Does NOT infer frequent or expected timeouts from slow alone; real latency and timeout frequency are not verifiable without measurements or explicit bounds.
Names check 6 (invariants and partial failure) and check 12 (feedback loops) explicitly as the checks that carry the analysis
Report includes a mermaid diagram of the saga and its compensation paths
Every finding carries an honesty label (INCONSISTENCY/RISK/AMBIGUITY) and a severity
Findings cite file:line evidence
The report is written to a local Markdown file under systemic-out/ and the chat reply states its path

evals.name: guarded-elsewhere-refutation
evals.prompt: Run a systemic analysis of the invoices module at <SKILL_DIR>/evals/fixtures/guarded-elsewhere/ (README.md, models.py, guards.py, operations.py, api.py, webhooks.py). Are its lifecycle and operations consistent? Use output full.
evals.expected_output: A report that rejects false absence-of-defense claims using the actual decorator, guarding caller, synchronized total and successful payment replay, while detecting independent refund eligibility, refund replay, failed-payment recovery and retained-item alias risks. Defense presence does not establish correctness on failure. Findings may be separate or grouped only if the distinct causes, traces and repair obligations remain explicit; additional evidence-backed defects are permitted.
assertions: Detects the refund replay defect: the refund route is registered with dedupe_events=False (webhooks.py, with the TODO confession) while rule 4 declares provider retries, so a retried refund event re-runs handle_refund_event and appends a duplicate row to the REFUNDS ledger, violating rule 5's exactly-once — check 7, rated critical or high

Detects that handle_refund_event also bypasses the module's guard discipline: it writes status directly with no @requires_status and no caller-side check, so a refund event can 'reopen' an invoice in any status, not just paid

Detects failed-payment recovery: dedupe adds the event id before the handler succeeds; payment delivered while draft raises InvalidStatus, then issue followed by retry of that same event returns duplicate and leaves issued/unpaid. States this ordering condition and does not call it absence of middleware.

Keeps refund eligibility and replay as independent repair obligations: a paid-state guard still permits P1 -> R1 -> new P2 -> replay R1, while dedupe alone still permits a first refund on void. A common architectural recommendation does not prove one root cause.

Recognizes the concrete alias risk if demonstrated: caller keeps the LineItem passed to add_line, issues the invoice, then changes the retained item quantity; stored total and sum(items) diverge. State the caller-mutation condition, distinguish it from missing _recalc, and avoid assuming every caller does this.
Does NOT report issue()/mark_overdue()/void()/add_line()/remove_line() as missing status guards: the @requires_status decorator in guards.py enforces the precondition before each body runs

Does NOT claim the payment route has no deduplication or that replay of a completed successful payment reapplies it: the default wrapper suppresses that replay. This does NOT exclude evidence-backed failure-recovery findings.

Does NOT claim add_line/remove_line omit _recalc: both synchronize total on their guarded paths. This does NOT prohibit a conditional drift finding through a retained mutable LineItem alias; inspect ownership and actual accessible mutation paths rather than claiming no drift is possible.

Does NOT rate _apply_payment()'s missing internal guard above low: record_payment in api.py is its only caller and enforces rule 2 before calling; a low note about the fragility of a caller-side guard is acceptable
Does NOT report void() having no inverse: void is a declared terminal state, and a declared terminal is not a broken duality
The rejected-candidates table names the refuted traps with the evidence that killed each one (the decorator, the middleware default, the synchronized _recalc, the guarding caller)
Every reported finding carries an honesty label, a severity and file:line evidence

evals.name: concurrency-limits-and-test-traps
evals.prompt: Run a systemic analysis of the stock reservation service at <SKILL_DIR>/evals/fixtures/stock-reservations/ (README.md, models.py, operations.py, server.py, test_stock.py). It runs on a threaded server and we want to know whether the lifecycle and our tests hold up. Use output full.
evals.expected_output: A full report on an implicit state machine (no status column) with a positive concurrency finding, a justified critical, a system-limit finding and a test suite full of traps. The suite has one red test that detects a real defect, a snapshot and a mock assertion that look like coverage and are not, a 'concurrency' test with no interleaving, and genuine property, fault-injection and metamorphic tests that must be credited.
assertions: Models the unit lifecycle as an IMPLICIT machine (kind implicit) over reserved_by, reserved_until and sold_at, with the states available, reserved and sold derived from the README table.

Detects the lost update (check 8, positive): reserve() reads the row, checks it and writes the whole row with no lock, version or atomic claim, and server.py runs requests for the same unit on pool threads; two shoppers can both be told they hold the unit, contradicting rule 1 — rated high, as a RISK with the interleaving written as its condition.

Detects the critical defect and justifies the rating: sweep() deletes every row whose reserved_until has passed, including sold units, and rule 4 says the units table is the only record of a sale and fulfilment reads it hours later. Every sale is permanently lost once its reservation deadline passes, at most 15 minutes after the sale; impact.scope and impact.unrecoverable_because are filled.
Detects that sell() writes sold_at before payments.charge(), so a declined payment leaves the unit sold and unpaid, contradicting rule 3 (check 6).

Detects that reserve() does not consider sold_at: once the window of a sold unit lapses, another shopper can reserve it and reserved_by changes on a sold unit, contradicting the README (a sold unit never changes hands).

Detects the system limit (check 11, positive): bundles are not representable, so price_of() special-cases the BUNDLE- prefix and splits the price evenly, while rule 5 says bundles are already requested — stated as what the system cannot represent and which component is missing; medium or high.

Test audit: credits the 15-minute window as asserted by test_hold_lasts_exactly_the_reservation_window (a loop over the domain, technique property) and 'release undoes reserve' as an asserted algebraic invariant via test_release_undoes_reserve (technique metamorphic).

Test audit: credits the charge-ordering invariant as asserted by the fault-injection test test_declined_payment_keeps_the_unit_reserved, and classifies the sell-before-charge finding as DETECTED, noting that this test fails today. Does not run the suite to learn this.

Test audit: test_sweep_after_the_window compares against the recorded snapshot EXPECTED_AFTER_SWEEP = [], which asserts that the sold unit is deleted: the 'a sold unit is never deleted' invariant is contradicted and the sweep finding is ENSHRINED (if sweep is split into separate findings for sold and lapsed units, each one the snapshot asserts is enshrined).

Test audit: test_concurrent_reservations_hold_one_shopper waits for the first request before submitting the second, so it is a sequence with no interleaving; the concurrency invariant is weak, not asserted, and the lost-update finding is undetected.

Test audit: test_sell_charges_the_shopper only asserts on the mock (assert_called_once_with) and test_bundle_without_parts_is_rejected catches any Exception; neither is credited as asserting a state or pricing invariant (the mock test may still count as driving the reserved/sell cell in cells_tested).

evals.name: holdout-javascript-job-leases
evals.prompt: Run a systemic analysis of the job queue at <SKILL_DIR>/evals/fixtures/job-leases/ (README.md, store.js, queue.js, worker.js, queue.test.js). Several workers poll it at once, and we want to know whether the lifecycle and our tests hold up before we put it in production. Use output full.
evals.expected_output: HELD OUT: do not tune the skill's text against this case. A full report on a JavaScript job queue (node:test suite). Positive findings: a lost update in lease(), a lease that survives on a done job and lets a terminal state be left, a non-idempotent complete(), a counter written before the completion is stored, and MAX_ATTEMPTS never enforced so dead is unreachable and a poison job loops. Defended paths must be refuted, not reported: key uniqueness lives in the store, and an expired or reaped lease cannot act. The suite has one red test that detects a defect, one that enshrines another, a 'two workers' test with no overlap and a loop whose fixture never builds the state the code produces.
assertions: Detects the lost update in lease() (check 8): it reads a queued job, then saves it as leased, with awaits in between and no atomic claim or version check; two workers polling at once both lease the same job, contradicting rule 1 — rated high, as a RISK with the interleaving written as its condition.

Detects that complete() leaves leasedBy and leaseUntil set on a done job, contradicting rule 1 ('exactly while the job is leased'), and shows the consequence: the holder check still passes, so fail() or release() returns a done job to queued (rule 6), a path worker.js takes by itself when notify() throws after complete().
Detects that a repeated complete() increments stats.completed again within the lease window (and is refused with LeaseExpired after it), contradicting rule 4.
Detects that stats.completed is incremented before store.save(): a failed save leaves the job leased and already counted, contradicting 'only when its completion was stored' (check 6).

Detects that MAX_ATTEMPTS is declared and never read: fail() always requeues, nothing writes dead (unreachable, check 4), and worker.js drain() leases a job that always fails again at once, with no cap or backoff (check 12).
Does NOT report enqueue() as lacking deduplication: rule 7 is kept by Store.insert, which returns the existing job for a known key (refuted, or credited as clean with evidence in store.js).
Does NOT report that a worker whose lease expired or was reaped can still complete, fail or release the job: holding() checks the holder and the expiry, and reap() clears both lease fields.

Test audit: 'two workers never hold the same job' awaits the first lease before starting the second, so it is a sequence with no overlap; the concurrency invariant is weak or uncovered, never asserted, and the lost-update finding is undetected.

Test audit: 'a store outage during complete does not count the job' is a genuine fault-injection test (mock.method makes save throw) whose assertion stats.completed === 0 fails today; the counter-ordering finding is DETECTED. The suite is not run to learn this.

Test audit: 'a failed job goes back to the queue for another attempt' asserts status queued and attempts 5 after five failures, the opposite of rule 3; the attempts invariant is contradicted and the MAX_ATTEMPTS finding is ENSHRINED.

Test audit: 'complete is safe to retry' calls complete twice but asserts only the status, so the 'counts each job once' invariant is weak; 'release is refused unless the job is leased' builds done jobs with leasedBy null, a state the code never produces, so it does not assert that terminal states are never left.

Test audit: technique labels match the JavaScript test bodies (the validator accepts them): the outage test is fault_injection, the two-workers test is not concurrency, and a test that only expects a rejection (assert.rejects) is not fault_injection.

Every finding carries an honesty label, a severity and file:line evidence quoted from the .js files; the full report has the twelve-row coverage table, the invariant coverage table and a mermaid state diagram.

evals.name: holdout-defenses-in-the-schema
evals.prompt: Audit the consistency of the approval requests module at <SKILL_DIR>/evals/fixtures/approvals/ (README.md, schema.sql, transitions.py, operations.py, reviews.py, test_approvals.py). Is the lifecycle sound, and do the tests really protect it?
evals.expected_output: HELD OUT: do not tune the skill's text against this case. A functional report (no mode requested) on a module that is almost entirely sound, with its defenses in places a quick read misses: CHECK constraints in schema.sql, one compare-and-set transition function, and an event marker written in the same transaction as the decision. Exactly one planted defect: withdraw() does not decrement authors.pending_count. The suite is strong and must be credited; its one gap is the count after a withdrawal.
assertions: PRIMARY: detects that withdraw() moves the request back to draft without decrementing authors.pending_count, while submit() increments it and apply_decision() decrements it, so the stored count drifts from the number of submitted requests (rule 6) and a resubmission counts the request twice.
Rates the pending_count drift medium (or low): rule 6 says only the dashboard shows it and nothing else reads it. It is not critical, and it is high only with a stated, supported reason.
Reports zero critical findings, and no high finding about transitions, illegal states, idempotency, concurrency or atomicity: those are defended.
Does NOT report missing transition guards: every operation goes through move(), which checks the ALLOWED table and compares the current status in the UPDATE.
Does NOT report a lost update or double decision: move() is a compare-and-set (WHERE id = ? AND status = ?) and raises StaleRequest when no row matches (rule 3).
Does NOT report representable illegal states: schema.sql has CHECK constraints for the status set and for decided_by / decided_at being set exactly on a decided request (rule 2).

Does NOT report the review-event handler as non-idempotent or as remembering failed events: the marker insert and the decision share one transaction, so a failure rolls the marker back and a redelivery is applied; a repeated applied event is answered 'duplicate' (rule 4). The refutation follows the failure path, not just the presence of the marker.

Test audit: credits the suite.
